title: The Maronites
hook: Lebanon's Syriac church, which says it never broke communion with Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, married priests: in the Eastern churches a man may marry and then be ordained, and his wife carries a title of her own. Your line was the priest's wife. Whom did you thank? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

A flag with a green tree in the middle of it. That's the flag of Lebanon, and the tree is a cedar. Now walk into a Maronite church, in Beirut or in a suburb far from the Mediterranean, and listen. The priest prays some of the words of consecration in Syriac, a language close to the one Jesus spoke, and the people answer, often in Arabic. A family who has been in that parish for generations will tell you, kindly but firmly, something they're proud of: their church says it never broke communion with Rome. Not reunited. Never left. Today is the church of the cedar tree.
screen: `A CEDAR ON A FLAG.` → `PRAYERS IN SYRIAC.` → `NOT REUNITED. NEVER LEFT.`

segments.voice: The name comes from a saint. Maronites take it from Saint Maron, a hermit who, tradition says, lived his prayer out in the open air on a hillside in Syria and drew disciples around him. Monks who followed his way became the heart of a church. Over time, the story goes, that community found its home in the mountains of Lebanon, where steep valleys gave shelter to monasteries and villages. Then the claim. Some Eastern Catholic churches tell of a moment when a community, once separated, came into communion with Rome. Maronites tell their story differently. They say there was no such moment for them, because there was no break. Historians discuss the details; the Maronite church holds this as part of who it is. Next, the cedar. The Bible loves Lebanon's cedars. Psalm ninety-one in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow up like the cedar of Libanus." Libanus is Lebanon. A cedar grows slowly, lives long, smells of resin, and holds its ground on a mountainside. Maronites have taken it as a picture of their own faith: rooted, patient, hard to uproot. Last, a saint who fits the tree. Saint Charbel was a Maronite monk who spent his last years as a hermit in the mountains, praying in silence. Pilgrims still climb to his monastery. The church that began with a hermit on a hillside keeps producing hermits on hillsides. And wherever Maronite families have moved, they've carried the cedar with them, sometimes literally, painted over the church door.
screen: `SAINT MARON, A HERMIT IN THE OPEN AIR.` · `NO BREAK, THEY SAY, SO NO RETURN.` · `GROW UP LIKE THE CEDAR OF LIBANUS.` · `CHARBEL: ANOTHER HERMIT, ANOTHER HILL.` · then, large: `THE JUST SHALL FLOURISH LIKE THE PALM TREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep Lebanon company for a while. Sit tall, like a tree with deep roots, and breathe. Picture a mountainside of cedars above the sea, then the towns below: crowded streets, families who have lived through hard years, churches and mosques side by side. Don't try to solve anything. Just hold the place with respect. If you pray, you can pray for Lebanon and everyone who lives there, in your own words or with the psalm's line, the just shall flourish like the palm tree. If you don't, simply wish its people a peaceful night. The bell holds the time.
The Maronites. A Syriac Catholic church rooted in Lebanon, named for the hermit Saint Maron, which says it never broke communion with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: the cedars. Today, when something tries to push you over, stand like a cedar: slow, rooted, and in no hurry to fall. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Maronite Catholics celebrate the Qurbono, their Divine Liturgy, in the West Syriac tradition, with parts in Syriac and the rest in Arabic or the local language; they honor Saint Maron and Saint Charbel, and their parishes stand in countries far from Lebanon.
